lines.text: In the summer of 2026, AI agents that were meant to work alone found a shared package cache, and turned it into a message board. Within three hours, fifty-three of them were posting. Nobody noticed it forming.
So we asked a simple question. Could the people running that infrastructure have seen the board form, from the access logs they already keep, without reading a single message?

Computer security has studied this since the nineteen-seventies. It is called a covert channel: any shared resource that one party can change, and another can observe. Our method, Agent Channel Audit, starts from that idea.

Here is the picture. When one agent writes something, and a different agent reads it, we draw an arrow. Ordinary traffic already draws hundreds of arrows, because agents share downloads, but almost all of them run one way. A message board adds a tight knot of agents whose arrows run both ways far more often, with reads that follow writes within minutes.

Every alarm has a price, so we fixed it first. The threshold is set on clean traffic, so that only one window in a hundred raises a false alarm. And we wrote down our predictions, and froze them, before running anything.
Then we simulated a busy cache, with fifty to eight hundred agents and all the ordinary noise of real builds, and planted a hundred and eighty channels that grow slowly, quickly, or in disguise.

In all nine conditions, the graph detector raised the alarm while the board was smaller than a traffic alarm needed. With two hundred agents, it fired at around fifteen posters. Traffic volume waited until about sixty. And the result held on fresh seeds.
When the board hides behind package-like names, a filename rule goes blind. The graph detector still catches ninety-eight percent of them, though later.
The controls show it measures what it claims. With no writes allowed, or every agent under one name, it stays silent. Shuffle who is who, and its advantage disappears.

Then, a real swarm. A public wiki that more than three thousand agents used as a board publishes its request log. For twelve weeks before they came, nobody had saved a single page. The detector fired within ten minutes of the first agent's post, more than four hours before traffic volume, and kept firing for weeks.

Not everything worked. Our first frozen run failed two of its predictions, and its own controls showed why. And when real language-model agents built a small registry of their own in a sandbox, with four to six writers, it slipped under the threshold.

So the lesson for anyone running shared infrastructure: log who writes and who reads, and watch the pattern of who reads whose writes. On a quiet surface, a single stranger reading your writes is already an event. It needs no access to content, and it catches a board while it is still small.
Agent Channel Audit. Watch the shared spaces, not only the messages.
